name: Cetrimonium chloride

lead: Cetrimonium chloride is a widely used conditioner ingredient that softens hair, reduces static and makes it easier to detangle, so hair looks smoother and more manageable after washing.

Its positively charged head binds to negatively charged hair, and combined with fatty alcohols and water it forms a creamy gel that coats the strands. It is used as part of the whole conditioner formula, and it has not been studied on its own for appearance outcomes.

paras: People get it by using conditioners or leave-in products that list it, typically applied after shampooing. It is usually paired with fatty alcohols such as stearyl alcohol, and the softer, easier-to-comb feel is immediate.

Dermatology reviews list it among quaternary ammonium compounds reported as contact irritants or allergens. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel is reported to have considered it safe in rinse-off products and at up to 0.25 percent in leave-on products. Concentrated forms are corrosive and toxic to aquatic life.

angle.text: Cetrimonium chloride is a conditioner surfactant that coats the hair, making it easier to detangle and softer to the touch so it looks smoother and more manageable after washing. You get the effect through the conditioner formula, and contact-allergy reports are documented.

lead: Cetrimonium chloride (cetyltrimethylammonium chloride, CTAC) is a quaternary ammonium cationic surfactant used in hair conditioners, where it makes hair easier to comb and smoother and softer to the touch. By coating the fibre, it reduces tangling, flyaways and static, so hair looks sleeker and shinier and is handled with less breakage during brushing.[1][2][3]

It binds to the negatively charged surface of hair left after shampooing. Wikipedia's conditioner entry describes cationic surfactants such as cetrimonium chloride, behentrimonium chloride and stearalkonium chloride as the main conditioning agents: they attach head-first to the fibre with their fatty tails facing outward, which flattens cuticle scales, reduces static and gives oils and silicones a surface to deposit on.[3] In conditioners it is typically combined with long-chain fatty alcohols such as stearyl alcohol; the mixture forms a lamellar gel with water, with cationic surfactant levels of about 1 to 2 percent.[1] It is also classed as a topical antiseptic and surfactant.[1]

Grokipedia reports that the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel considered it safe in rinse-off products and at up to 0.25 percent in leave-on products when formulated to limit irritation.[2] Dermatology literature lists it among quaternary ammonium compounds reported as contact allergens or irritants in some people, and patch-test series include it as a screening allergen.[4][5][6]

paras: In hair conditioners and some shampoos, the surfactant is combined with fatty alcohols. The surfactant, fatty alcohol and water form a lamellar structure that creates a percolated network, giving conditioners their gel-like texture.[1] The fatty alcohol concentration is usually equal to or higher than that of the surfactant.[1]

Wikipedia's conditioner entry explains the underlying need: shampoo's anionic surfactants strip surface lipids and leave hair rougher and more negatively charged, so cationic conditioning agents are applied afterward to neutralise that charge. It says longer alkyl chains generally produce larger reductions in wet combing force, and that conditioners do not repair hair biologically, because hair is dead tissue; they coat the fibre and fill defects in the cuticle.[3] Rinse-out conditioners, deep conditioning masks and leave-in products are the common formats.[3]

Beyond hair conditioners, it is classed as a topical antiseptic and surfactant (ATC codes D08AJ02 and R02AA17) and is listed with quaternary ammonium antiseptics such as benzalkonium, cetylpyridinium and benzethonium chloride.[1] Grokipedia also lists industrial biocide and phase-transfer catalyst roles.[2]

The compound has formula C19H42ClN and a molar mass of about 320 g/mol; its systematic name is N,N,N-trimethylhexadecan-1-aminium chloride, with a 16-carbon (cetyl) chain.[1] It belongs to the cetrimonium salts, which include cetrimonium bromide, and behentrimonium chloride is a longer-chain analogue.[1] An analytical study described a method for measuring cetrimonium chloride and fatty alcohols together in hair conditioners.[7]

A 2023 review of quaternary ammonium compounds and contact dermatitis lists cetrimonium chloride, along with benzalkonium chloride, cetrimonium bromide and others, among compounds identified as potential culprits of skin sensitivity, and notes that exposure rose during the COVID-19 pandemic as these compounds became active ingredients in many disinfectants. The authors state that additional research is needed to classify their dermal effects.[4]

The North American Contact Dermatitis Group's 2019-2020 data included cetrimonium chloride at 0.5 percent among allergens with the highest proportion of doubtful patch test reactions at the final visit (3.4 percent).[5] A Thai survey of 6,864 personal care products from 2010 to 2024 examined surfactant prevalence against patch-test reactivity.[6] Grokipedia reports that the concentrated substance is classed as causing severe skin burns and eye damage and as very toxic to aquatic life.[2]
Animal studies of ophthalmic preservatives, including cetrimonium chloride, have examined effects on the conjunctiva; these concern eye drops, not hair products.[8]
No studies found of its effect on hair appearance as a single ingredient. Related literature includes contact-dermatitis reviews and patch-test studies of quaternary ammonium compounds.[4][5][6]
